title: The Wrongness Tax
author: Scott D. Clary
summary: Clary opens with a stark observation: you are wrong about something important right now. There is a belief you hold, a position you have defended, a decision you have justified that no longer holds up. Evidence has been accumulating and cracks are showing. But you haven't admitted it yet, waiting for the right moment when admitting it won't cost as much. That moment never comes. Every day you wait, the cost goes up. This is the wrongness tax: the compounding cost of not admitting error. The longer you hold a false position, the more your credibility, trust, and clarity suffer. The remedy is direct: admit it now, while the cost is still low. The earlier you acknowledge error, the smaller the cost.
points: Everyone is currently wrong about something; the question is not whether error exists, but when you will acknowledge it.
The cost of admitting wrongness increases each day you delay; waiting for a convenient moment ensures the moment never comes and costs mount.
Holding a false position damages credibility, trust with others, and your own clarity about what you actually know.
The wrongness tax compounds: the longer the gap between when you know something is wrong and when you admit it, the more expensive the admission becomes.
Acknowledging error early, while stakes and costs are low, preserves trust and opens the door to course correction.
quotes: You're wrong about something important right now. You've probably known for a while. Maybe months. Maybe longer. There's a belief you hold, a position you've defended, a decision you've justified that doesn't quite hold up anymore.
The evidence has been accumulating. The cracks are showing.
But you haven't admitted it yet. You're waiting for the right moment. A moment when admitting it won't cost as much.
That moment never comes. Every day you wait, the cost goes up.
The longer you carry a false position, the more you have to reconstruct when you finally let it go.
Your credibility, trust with others, and your own clarity all suffer when you maintain a false position longer than necessary.” Archived from Scott D. Clary Newsletter on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
